verification_candidates.claim_text: Consistency in bed and wake times matters more for sleep than the exact number of hours slept.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: Probably that consistency matters more than the exact number of hours
verification_candidates.rationale: A comparative claim about what drives sleep quality that can be checked against sleep research.

verification_candidates.claim_text: Sleeping in on weekends produces a mini jet lag effect on Monday, which some people call social jet lag.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: that is basically a mini jet lag every Monday, some people call it social jet lag
verification_candidates.rationale: A named causal effect of weekend sleep-ins that can be checked against circadian research.

verification_candidates.claim_text: Social jet lag happens to almost everyone who sleeps in a lot on weekends and is very common.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: It happens to almost everyone who sleeps in a lot on weekends, it is really common
verification_candidates.rationale: A prevalence claim about how widespread social jet lag is.

verification_candidates.claim_text: The bigger reason screens before bed disturb sleep is that scrolling keeps the brain engaged and alert, rather than the light itself.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: the light matters some but the bigger issue is usually that scrolling keeps your brain engaged and alert instead of winding down
verification_candidates.rationale: A claim about the relative causal role of light versus mental engagement that research can check.

verification_candidates.claim_text: Stopping screen use twenty to thirty minutes before bed helps people fall asleep somewhat faster on average.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: Even cutting it down to twenty or thirty minutes before bed seems to help people fall asleep a bit faster on average.
verification_candidates.rationale: A specific dose of screen avoidance with a stated sleep-onset benefit that is checkable.

verification_candidates.claim_text: Short naps of about twenty minutes are usually harmless and can improve alertness later in the day.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: Short naps, like twenty minutes, are usually fine and can actually help alertness later in the day.
verification_candidates.rationale: A specific nap length with a claimed alertness benefit that can be checked against nap studies.

verification_candidates.claim_text: Longer naps, especially late in the afternoon, can make it harder to fall asleep that night.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: Longer naps can mess with your ability to fall asleep that night
verification_candidates.rationale: A causal claim about long and late naps impairing night-time sleep onset.

verification_candidates.claim_text: Melatonin can help a little for occasional jet lag or a temporary schedule shift.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: For occasional jet lag or a temporary schedule shift it can help a little
verification_candidates.rationale: A benefit claim about melatonin for a specific indication that trials can check.

verification_candidates.claim_text: People often take much more melatonin than they need.

verification_candidates.rationale: A claim about typical melatonin dosing relative to need that dosing data can check.

verification_candidates.claim_text: Most people would do fine with a much smaller melatonin dose than the doses sold in stores.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: Most people would probably do fine with a much smaller dose than what is sold in stores.
verification_candidates.rationale: A dosing claim that could change how much melatonin listeners take.

verification_candidates.claim_text: Getting daylight in the morning, even ten minutes outside, helps set the body clock for the whole day.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: Get some daylight in the morning, even just ten minutes outside, it helps set your clock for the whole day.
verification_candidates.rationale: A specific light-exposure dose with a circadian effect that can be checked.

verification_candidates.claim_text: Being outside on a cloudy morning is far brighter than any indoor lighting.
verification_candidates.evidence_quote: even a cloudy morning outside is way brighter than any indoor lighting
verification_candidates.rationale: A comparison of outdoor and indoor light levels that measurement can check.
